items.title: Tax in a digital world
items.rule:
Businesses now sell across borders without being physically present: online retail, remote education, streaming. Two questions follow:

  • Which country should tax the profit?
  • What happens when several countries all try to tax the same profit?
items.body:
Residence gets harder to pin down: should a business be resident where its head office is if most income comes from customers elsewhere?

Ethics angle: directors choosing low-tax jurisdictions purely to cut tax are avoiding (legal), not evading, but face reputational risk.
items.upd: Several countries (UK 2% Digital Services Tax since 2020, France, Italy) tax digital revenue while the OECD "Pillar One" deal on taxing where customers are is negotiated.

items.title: Corporate residence
items.rule:
A resident company is normally taxed on its worldwide income. Residence is decided by either:

  • place of incorporation, or
  • place of central management and control (where the board meets and decides)

Generally the country of control wins.
items.trap: Where customers, suppliers, factories or a stock-exchange listing are has nothing to do with residence.

items.q: Which of the following would NOT normally be used to decide where a company is resident for tax purposes?
opts: Where central management and control is exercised
The country in which it was registered
Where its directors hold their board meetings
Where most of its customers are located
sol: Residence tests: incorporation (registration) or central management and control (board meetings).
Customer location is not a test.

alt.q: Which of the following IS normally used to decide where a company is resident for tax purposes?
opts: Where most of its customers are located
Where its largest supplier is based
Where its directors hold their board meetings
Where its shares are listed
sol: Board meetings = central management and control, a residence test.
Customers, suppliers and listings are not.

items.q: Which would NOT normally be used to decide where a company is resident for tax?
opts: Where its board meetings are held
Where it is incorporated
Where central management and control is exercised
Where its largest supplier is based
sol: Incorporation and control (board meetings, central management) are the tests. Supplier location is irrelevant.

items.title: OECD model: permanent establishment
items.rule:
Business profits are taxable in another country only if the company has a permanent establishment (PE) there.

Place of managementBranch
OfficeFactory
WorkshopMine, oil/gas well, quarry
Building site lasting more than 12 months

Not a PE: facilities used only for storage, display or delivery; building sites of 12 months or less.
items.trap: A warehouse used only to store goods is the classic wrong option. So is a 9- or 10-month construction project.
items.upd: The 2017 OECD Model narrowed the storage/display exemption to activities that are preparatory or auxiliary. The 12-month site rule is unchanged. Exam answers are unaffected.

items.q: Under the OECD model, a company's business profits are taxable in another country only if the company has a ______ in that country.
opts: shareholder resident
permanent establishment
registered office for its AGM
customer base
sol: OECD Article 7: business profits are taxable abroad only through a permanent establishment.

alt.q: Under the OECD model, which of the following would by itself allow Country F to tax a foreign company's business profits?
opts: Many of the company's customers live in Country F
The company has a factory in Country F
Some of the company's shareholders live in Country F
The company holds its AGM in Country F once
sol: A factory is a permanent establishment, so Country F can tax the profits it generates.
Customers, shareholders or a one-off meeting do not create a PE.

items.q: Which of the following is NOT specifically listed as a permanent establishment under the OECD model?
opts: A branch
A workshop
A quarry
A building site that lasts {m} months
sol: Branch, workshop and quarry (a place of extracting natural resources) are all listed.
A building site is a PE only if it lasts more than 12 months. {m} months is too short.

alt.q: Which of the following IS specifically listed as a permanent establishment under the OECD model?
opts: A facility used only to store goods
A building site lasting 8 months
A facility used only to display goods
A workshop
sol: A workshop is on the list.
Storage-only, display-only and sites of 12 months or less are not PEs.

items.q: Which of the following would be a permanent establishment under the OECD model? I. A place of management. II. A facility used only to display goods. III. A gas well. IV. A construction project lasting ten months. V. A workshop.
opts: All of them
I and V
I, III, IV and V
I, III and V
sol: PE: place of management (I), gas well (III), workshop (V).
Not PE: display-only facility (II); construction lasting 12 months or less (IV).
items.trap: Option C counts the 10-month project. It needs to exceed 12 months.

alt.q: Which of the following would be a permanent establishment under the OECD model? I. A branch. II. A warehouse used only for storage. III. A construction project lasting 14 months. IV. A mine. V. A facility used only for delivery.
opts: I, III and IV
I and IV
All of them
I, II, III and IV
sol: PE: branch (I), construction over 12 months (III), mine (IV).
Storage-only (II) and delivery-only (V) facilities are not PEs.

items.q: Under the OECD model, which would NOT normally create a permanent establishment?
opts: A branch office
A dependent agent who regularly signs contracts for the company
A factory
A facility used only to store and display goods
sol: Branches, factories and dependent agents habitually concluding contracts create a PE.
Storage/display-only facilities do not.

items.title: Dual residence: the tie-breaker
items.rule: If two countries both treat a company as resident, the OECD tie-breaker makes it resident where its place of effective management is: where the board makes its key decisions.

ex.title: Nova Ltd
ex.given: Incorporated in P. Factories and sales in Q. Board meets and decides strategy in R. All OECD treaties.
steps: Where it trades or sells (Q) is not a residence test.

items.trap: Picking the country where it trades or makes its profits. The tie-breaker ignores that.

items.q: Tarn Co is incorporated in Country P. Its factories are in Country Q. Its board meets and makes all strategic decisions in Country R. Its shares are listed on a stock exchange in Country S. All four countries follow the OECD model. Where is Tarn Co resident for tax?
opts: Country Q
Country P
Country R
Country S
sol: OECD tie-breaker: place of effective management.
The board decides strategy in R, so Tarn is resident in R.
Factories (Q) may create a PE there, but that is not residence.
items.trap: Q: a factory creates a permanent establishment, not residence.

alt.q: Tarn Co is incorporated in Country P. Its factories are in Country R. Its shares are listed on a stock exchange in Country Q. Its board meets and makes all strategic decisions in Country S. All four countries follow the OECD model. Where is Tarn Co resident for tax?
opts: Country Q
Country P
Country R
Country S
sol: Place of effective management = where the board makes strategic decisions = Country S.
Incorporation (P), factories (R) and listing (Q) don't decide it.

items.q: Lomond Co: (i) is incorporated in Country X; (ii) has its directors meet and exercise control in Country Y, though it does no trading there; (iii) carries out its main trade in Country Z. All three countries have OECD-model treaties with each other. Where is Lomond resident for tax?
opts: Country X
Country Y
Country Z
Countries Y and Z
sol: Control and effective management are in Y.
Doing no trading in Y doesn't matter; residence follows control.
items.trap: Thinking it can't be resident somewhere it doesn't trade.

alt.q: Lomond Co: (i) is incorporated in Country Y; (ii) has its directors meet and exercise control in Country Z, where it also does some trading; (iii) carries out its main trade in Country X. All three countries have OECD-model treaties with each other. Where is Lomond resident for tax?
sol: Control and effective management are in Z, so Lomond is resident in Z.
Main trade in X creates a PE there, not residence.

items.q: Fenwick Co is incorporated in Country 1 and trades mainly in Country 2. Its board and effective management are in Country 3. All three have OECD-model treaties. Where is Fenwick resident for tax?
opts: Country 1
Country 2
Country 3
Both Country 2 and Country 3
sol: Place of effective management = Country 3.

alt.q: Fenwick Co is incorporated in Country 3 and trades mainly in Country 1. Its board and effective management are in Country 2. All three have OECD-model treaties. Where is Fenwick resident for tax?
sol: Place of effective management = Country 2.

items.q: FZ is incorporated in Country X and makes most of its sales in Country Y. Its board meets in, and effective management is run from, Country Z. All three countries have OECD-based treaties. Where is FZ resident?
opts: Country X
Country Y
Country Z
Both Y and Z
sol: The tie-breaker is the place of effective management: Z.

alt.q: FZ is incorporated in Country Z and makes most of its sales in Country X. Its board meets in, and effective management is run from, Country Y. All three countries have OECD-based treaties. Where is FZ resident?
opts: Country X
Country Y
Country Z
Both X and Z
sol: Effective management is in Y.

items.title: Double taxation and the three reliefs
items.rule:
Double taxation: the same income taxed where it arises and again where the taxpayer is resident. Treaties relieve it, but often not completely.

MethodHow
ExemptionIncome exempt (wholly or partly) in one country
Tax creditForeign tax credited against home tax, capped at the lower of foreign tax and home tax on that income
DeductionForeign tax deducted from the income; only the net is taxed at home. Least generous.
items.trap: Group loss relief is not a double tax relief method. It's a domestic group rule.

items.q: Double taxation arises:
opts: when group companies surrender losses to each other
when the same income is taxed both in the country where it arises and in the taxpayer's country of residence
when tax losses are carried forward against future profits
when a gain is relieved because the proceeds are reinvested
sol: Source country taxes because the income arose there; residence country taxes worldwide income.

alt.q: Which of the following is an example of double taxation?
opts: A trading loss surrendered to another group company
Royalty income taxed in the country it is earned and again in the recipient's country of residence
Two companies in the same group each paying tax on their own profits
A gain postponed by rollover relief
sol: The same income taxed in two countries = double taxation.

items.q: The purpose of double taxation relief is to:
opts: make sure no income is ever taxed more than once
reduce the double taxation of income earned overseas
stop dividends between group companies in the same country being taxed twice
give relief when a company's tax rate is twice the normal rate
sol: DTR mitigates double taxation on overseas income. It often doesn't remove it completely (e.g. the deduction method).
items.trap: A overstates it: "ensure never" is too strong.

alt.q: Which statement about double taxation relief is correct?
opts: It always removes double taxation completely
Under the credit method, relief is capped at the home tax on that income
It applies only to dividends between companies in the same country
It refunds foreign tax that exceeds home tax
sol: Credit relief = lower of foreign tax and home tax on that income.
Excess foreign tax isn't refunded, so relief doesn't always remove double tax.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the deduction method of double tax relief?
opts: The foreign tax is deducted as an expense in the statement of profit or loss
The foreign tax is treated as a trading loss
The foreign tax is deducted from the foreign income, so only the net amount is taxed in the country of residence
The foreign tax is deducted from sales revenue
sol: Deduction relief: net foreign income (after foreign tax) is taxed at home.

alt.q: Which statement correctly describes the credit method of double tax relief?
opts: The foreign tax is deducted from the foreign income, so only the net is taxed at home
Foreign tax is set against home tax on that income, up to the amount of the home tax
The foreign income is exempt in the home country
The foreign tax is treated as a trading loss
sol: Credit relief: home tax on the gross income, less a credit for foreign tax, capped at the home tax.
A is deduction; C is exemption.

items.q: Which is NOT a method of double tax relief?
opts: Deduction relief
Exemption
Tax credit relief
Group loss relief
sol: The three DTR methods are exemption, credit and deduction. Group loss relief is a domestic group rule.

items.title: The three reliefs as formulas
items.rule: Income I, foreign rate f, home rate h Exemption: total = f·I Credit: home pays max(0, (h − f)·I) total = max(f, h)·I Deduction: total = f·I + h·(1 − f)·I

steps: Credit: home tax 30,000 − credit 20,000 = 10,000; total 30,000 = the higher rate.

items.trap: Under credit relief, if f > h the excess foreign tax is simply lost. The home country never refunds it.

items.q: A company resident in Country H earns ${I} of income in Country F, where it pays tax at {f%}. Country H taxes residents at {h%} and gives credit relief for foreign tax. How much tax does the company pay in Country H on this income?
sol: Home tax on gross income: {I} × {h%} = {=I*h}
Credit = lower of foreign tax {=I*f} and home tax {=I*h} = {=min(I*f,I*h)}
Home tax payable = {=max(0,(h-f)*I)}{?f>h| (the extra {=(f-h)*I} of foreign tax goes unrelieved)|}
items.trap: {?f>h|Entering a negative number. The credit is capped at the home tax; no refund.|Paying the full {=I*h}: the credit for foreign tax comes off.}

items.q: A company resident in Country H earns ${I} of income in Country F, where it pays tax at {f%}. Country H taxes residents at {h%} and gives relief only by the deduction method. What is the TOTAL tax (both countries) on this income?
sol: Foreign tax = {I} × {f%} = {=f*I}
Net income taxed at home = {=I*(1-f)} × {h%} = {=h*(1-f)*I}
Total = {=f*I + h*(1-f)*I}
items.trap: Taxing the gross {I} at home. Deduction relief taxes only the net after foreign tax.

items.title: Overseas branch v subsidiary
items.rule:
SubsidiaryBranch
StatusSeparate entity, resident abroadPart of the parent
Parent taxed onDividends received onlyAll branch profits as they arise
LossesNo group reliefAvailable to the parent straight away
Tax depreciationForeign rules onlyParent claims on branch assets
Asset transfersMay trigger a gainNo gain / no loss
items.body: Rule of thumb: branch for a new operation expecting early losses; subsidiary for a profitable operation in a lower-tax country.
items.trap: Saying a branch is taxed only on profits remitted home. That's the subsidiary (via dividends). Branch profits are taxed as they arise.

items.q: A resident company trades overseas through a branch. Which of the following does NOT usually apply?
opts: Assets can be moved to the branch without a capital gain arising
Tax is charged only on the profits the branch sends home
Capital allowances can be claimed on the branch's qualifying assets
Branch losses can be set against the company's other profits straight away
sol: A branch is part of the company, so all its profits are taxed as they arise, not just remittances.
A, C and D are standard branch features.

alt.q: A resident company trades overseas through a subsidiary. Which of the following usually applies?
opts: Assets can be moved to the subsidiary without a capital gain arising
The parent is taxed only on dividends it receives from the subsidiary
The parent claims capital allowances on the subsidiary's assets
Subsidiary losses can be set against the parent's profits straight away
sol: A foreign subsidiary is a separate taxpayer abroad. The parent is taxed only on what it receives as dividends.
A, C and D are branch features.

items.q: Which is the best definition of an overseas subsidiary?
opts: A division of the parent company that trades abroad
A company resident for tax in one country whose shares are owned (controlled) by a company resident in another country
Any company with foreign shareholders
A permanent establishment of the parent abroad
sol: A subsidiary is a separate company, resident abroad, controlled by the parent.
A and D describe a branch / PE.

items.q: For each feature, choose whether it applies to an overseas branch or an overseas subsidiary.
items: Losses can be used against the parent's profits straight away
The parent is taxed only on dividends received
Assets move from the parent at no gain / no loss
Suits a profitable operation in a lower-tax country
sol: Branch = part of the parent: losses usable immediately, assets move at no gain / no loss.
Subsidiary = separate taxpayer: parent taxed on dividends only, so low-tax profits can be kept abroad.

items.title: Withholding tax v underlying tax
items.rule:
Withholding tax (WHT)Deducted at source by the paying country from interest, royalties, rent or dividends paid abroad. Recipient gets gross − WHT.
Underlying tax (UT)The corporate tax already paid on the profits a dividend comes out of.
UT = gross dividend × (tax on profits ÷ profit after tax)
items.body: Both count as foreign tax for double tax relief.
items.trap: Trading profits the company earns itself are not subject to withholding tax. WHT is on payments made to foreign recipients.

items.q: Kell Co owns 30% of Rho Co, which is resident abroad. Rho pays Kell a dividend: Rho's tax authority deducts ${w} before payment, and Kell receives ${net2}. The ${w} is:
opts: corporate income tax
underlying tax
capital tax
withholding tax
sol: Tax deducted at source from a dividend before it is paid = withholding tax.
Underlying tax is the corporate tax already paid on Rho's profits.

items.q: Underlying tax is:
opts: tax withheld at source when a dividend is paid
the tax paid on the profits out of which a dividend is paid
the amount of double tax relief that can be claimed
tax paid in the country of residence on foreign income
sol: UT = corporate tax already suffered on the profits behind the dividend.
A is withholding tax.

opts: tax withheld at source when a dividend is paid
the tax paid on the profits out of which a dividend is paid
the amount of double tax relief that can be claimed
tax paid in the country of residence on foreign income
sol: WHT is deducted by the paying country at source.
B is underlying tax.

items.q: A withholding tax is:
opts: tax an employer deducts but never pays over
the tax due less any amount withheld
tax deducted at source before interest or dividends are paid
tax on increases in the value of investments
sol: Withholding = deducted at source before payment.

opts: tax an employer deducts but never pays over
the corporate tax paid on the profits a dividend is paid out of
tax deducted at source before interest or dividends are paid
tax on increases in the value of investments
sol: UT = corporate tax already suffered on the profits behind the dividend.
C is withholding tax.

items.q: Opal Co made a profit of ${pr} and paid tax of ${tx2}. It pays a gross dividend of ${gd} to its overseas parent, and {w%} is deducted when the dividend is paid. The {w%} is called:
opts: underlying tax
corporate income tax
foreign tax
withholding tax
sol: Deducted when the dividend is paid = withholding tax.
The ${tx2} tax on Opal's profit is what gives rise to underlying tax.
items.trap: C "foreign tax" is too vague: both WHT and UT are foreign taxes.

items.q: Which of these is normally NOT subject to withholding tax?
opts: Trading profits the company earns itself
Royalties paid to a foreign owner
Dividends paid to foreign shareholders
Interest paid to a foreign lender
sol: WHT applies to payments made to foreign recipients (royalties, dividends, interest).
A company's own trading profit is subject to corporate tax, not WHT.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes withholding tax from underlying tax?
opts: Withholding tax is deducted at source from a payment; underlying tax is the corporate tax already paid on the profits the dividend comes from
Withholding tax is the corporate tax on the subsidiary's profits; underlying tax is deducted when the dividend is paid
They are two names for the same tax
Withholding tax applies to companies; underlying tax applies to individuals
sol: WHT: deducted by the paying country from the payment itself.
UT: corporate tax suffered on the profits behind the dividend.

items.title: Computing foreign tax on a dividend
items.rule: WHT = gross dividend × w UT = gross dividend × T / PAT Gross foreign income = dividend + UT Cash received = dividend − WHT Foreign tax suffered = WHT + UT
items.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 320 210" role="img" aria-label="From subsidiary profit to dividend received: underlying tax and withholding tax">
<g font-size="10"><rect x="20" y="30" width="60" height="150" fill="#1f5fbf" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#1f5fbf"/><text x="50" y="22" text-anchor="middle">PBT 500</text>
<rect x="20" y="30" width="60" height="37.5" fill="#b42318" fill-opacity=".5"/><text x="50" y="52" text-anchor="middle">tax 125</text>
<rect x="110" y="67.5" width="60" height="112.5" fill="#1f5fbf" fill-opacity=".2" stroke="#1f5fbf"/><text x="140" y="60" text-anchor="middle">PAT 375</text>
<rect x="200" y="135" width="60" height="45" fill="#1f5fbf" fill-opacity=".45" stroke="#1f5fbf"/><text x="230" y="128" text-anchor="middle">Dividend 150</text>
<rect x="200" y="120" width="60" height="0" /><rect x="200" y="135" width="60" height="4.5" fill="#b42318"/><text x="268" y="142">WHT 15</text>
<rect x="270" y="90" width="40" height="15" fill="#b42318" fill-opacity=".5"/><text x="290" y="85" text-anchor="middle">UT 50</text>
<text x="160" y="200" text-anchor="middle">UT = 150 × 125/375 = 50 · gross = 150 + 50 = 200 · cash = 135</text></g></svg>
items.body: Shortcut when the sub pays tax at rate t and you know the dividend D: T/PAT = t/(1 − t), so UT = D·t/(1 − t) and D + UT = D/(1 − t), the pre-tax profit behind the dividend.

ex.title: HomeCo / OverCo
ex.given: OverCo (100% owned): PBT 500,000, tax 125,000, PAT 375,000. Dividend 150,000 with 10% WHT.

items.trap: Dividing by PBT instead of PAT. Dividends come out of after-tax profit.

items.q: A foreign subsidiary pays a gross dividend of ${gd} to its parent. The subsidiary's profit before tax was ${pbt}, and it paid tax of ${tx}. Calculate the underlying tax on the dividend, to the nearest $.
sol: Profit after tax = {pbt} − {tx} = {=pbt-tx}
UT = {gd} × {tx} / {=pbt-tx} = {=rd(gd*tx/(pbt-tx))}
items.trap: Using profit before tax as the denominator ({=rd(gd*tx/pbt)}).

items.q: A parent company receives a dividend of ${net} from a foreign subsidiary, after {w%} withholding tax. The subsidiary's profit before tax was ${pbt}, and it paid tax of ${tx}. How much foreign tax has been suffered on the dividend? Answer to the nearest $.
sol: Gross dividend = {net} ÷ (1 − {w%}) = {=net/(1-w)}
WHT = {=net/(1-w)} − {net} = {=net/(1-w)*w}
PAT = {=pbt-tx}; UT = {=net/(1-w)} × {tx}/{=pbt-tx} = {=net/(1-w)*tx/(pbt-tx)}
Total foreign tax = {=rd(net/(1-w)*w + net/(1-w)*tx/(pbt-tx))}
items.trap: Computing WHT as {w%} of the net {net}. The {w%} applies to the gross dividend, so gross up first.

items.title: Credit relief on a dividend; ownership %
items.rule: Home tax = gross foreign income × h DTR = min(WHT + UT, home tax) Payable = home tax − DTR

ex.title: HomeCo continued (gross 200,000; foreign tax 65,000)
steps: Home rate 30%: home tax 60,000; DTR = min(65,000, 60,000) = 60,000; payable 0. 5,000 of foreign tax is unrelieved.
Home rate 40%: home tax 80,000; DTR 65,000; payable 15,000.

items.trap: If the parent owns less than 100%, it only receives its share of the dividend. Apply WHT and UT to the parent's share, not the whole dividend.

items.q: Home Co owns {own%} of Overseas Co. Overseas Co's profit before tax is ${pbt}. It pays foreign corporate tax at {ft%} and distributes all of its after-tax profit. Withholding tax of {w%} is deducted from dividends paid abroad. Home Co pays tax at {h%} on the gross foreign income and gets credit relief for foreign taxes. Calculate the net dividend Home Co receives in cash.
sol: Overseas PAT = {pbt} × (1 − {ft%}) = {=pbt*(1-ft)}, all distributed
Home Co's {own%} share = {div}
WHT {w%} = {wht}
Cash received = {=div-wht}
items.trap: Using the whole dividend instead of Home Co's {own%} share.

items.q: Home Co owns {own%} of Overseas Co. Overseas Co's profit before tax is ${pbt}. It pays foreign corporate tax at {ft%} and distributes all of its after-tax profit. Withholding tax of {w%} is deducted from dividends paid abroad. Home Co pays tax at {h%} on the gross foreign income and gets credit relief for foreign taxes. Calculate the underlying tax on Home Co's dividend.
sol: Overseas tax = {=pbt*ft}; PAT = {=pbt*(1-ft)}
Home Co's dividend = {div}
UT = {div} × {=pbt*ft}/{=pbt*(1-ft)} = {ut}

items.q: Home Co owns {own%} of Overseas Co. Overseas Co's profit before tax is ${pbt}. It pays foreign corporate tax at {ft%} and distributes all of its after-tax profit. Withholding tax of {w%} is deducted from dividends paid abroad. Home Co pays tax at {h%} on the gross foreign income and gets credit relief for foreign taxes. Calculate Home Co's tax payable on the dividend.
sol: Dividend {div}; UT {ut}; gross income = {gross}
Home tax {h%} × {gross} = {home}
Foreign tax = WHT {wht} + UT {ut} = {ftot}
DTR = lower of {ftot} and {home}
Payable = {=max(0,home-ftot)}
items.trap: Taxing only the cash received. Home tax is on the gross income: dividend + underlying tax.

items.title: Transfer pricing
items.rule:
Sales, services or loans between group companies on non-arm's-length terms shift profit, usually to a lower-tax country.

Adjustment = quantity × (arm's-length price − transfer price) → added to the under-charging company's taxable profit
items.body:
Two forms of rule: (1) goods and services restated to an arm's-length (market) price; (2) loans: interest on debt beyond what an independent lender would give is disallowed (thin capitalisation).

Documentation of the transfer-pricing policy is a key record-keeping requirement for groups.

ex.given: Alpha (30% tax) sells 10,000 units to subsidiary Beta (10% tax) at $4. Market price $9.
steps: Alpha's taxable profit is increased by 50,000.

items.trap: Adjusting the low-tax company. The authority adjusts the company that gained the tax advantage by under-charging.

items.q: Brook sells {q} units to a related overseas company at ${tp#2} each. The same units sell to unrelated customers for ${mp#2} each. Transfer pricing rules apply. By how much is Brook's taxable profit increased?
sol: Arm's-length price = {mp#2}
Adjustment = {q} × ({mp#2} − {tp#2}) = {=q*(mp-tp)}

items.q: Parent P (tax 30%) sells goods to its subsidiary S (tax 12%) at well below market price. Under transfer pricing rules, what happens?
opts: S's taxable profit is reduced to market price
P's taxable profit is increased as if the sale were at market price
Both companies are taxed at 30%
Nothing, because group sales are exempt
sol: P under-charged, shifting profit to low-tax S.
The rules restate P's sale to the arm's-length price, increasing P's taxable profit.

alt.q: Parent P (tax 12%) BUYS goods from its subsidiary S (tax 30%) at well below market price. Under transfer pricing rules, whose taxable profit is adjusted upward?
opts: P's
S's
Neither
Both
sol: S is under-charging, shifting profit to low-tax P.
S's sales are restated to arm's length, so S's taxable profit goes up.

items.q: A parent funds its overseas subsidiary with a loan far larger than an independent bank would offer. The subsidiary deducts all the interest. How do thin capitalisation rules respond?
opts: The interest on the excess debt is disallowed for tax
The whole loan is treated as share capital and no interest is deductible
The subsidiary is taxed in the parent's country
The parent must charge a higher interest rate
sol: Only interest on debt beyond the arm's-length amount is disallowed (treated like a dividend).

items.title: Ethics of international tax
items.rule:
Using tax havens, aggressive transfer pricing or thin capitalisation is usually avoidance: legal, but it can wreck reputation ("not paying a fair share").

Evasion internationally: hiding income offshore, false invoices between group companies. Illegal.
items.body: Authorities' tools: transfer-pricing documentation, arm's-length rules, information exchange between tax authorities, thin cap rules.

items.q: Classify each as tax avoidance or tax evasion.
items: Moving the board and effective management to a low-tax country
Issuing false invoices from an overseas subsidiary to inflate expenses
Not declaring interest earned in an offshore bank account
Funding a subsidiary with debt to get interest deductions within the thin cap limit
sol: Legal restructuring (residence, permitted debt) = avoidance.
False documents and hidden income = evasion.

items.title: Global minimum tax (Pillar Two)
items.rule: About 140 countries agreed a 15% minimum effective rate for groups with revenue of €750m+. If a group's rate in a country is below 15%, a top-up tax applies: collected locally (domestic minimum tax) or by the parent's country (Income Inclusion Rule).
items.body:
UK: Multinational Top-up Tax for periods from 31 December 2023, plus a domestic top-up tax. A January 2026 "side-by-side" package mainly leaves US-parented groups under US rules.

Why it matters: it cuts the payoff from shifting profit to low-tax countries.
items.upd: This is outside the F1 syllabus and study text. It's here only as context for transfer pricing and tax havens.
